questions.question: A 60 y/o woman presents with abdominal pain localized to the upper right quadrant. Imaging reveals a mass adjacent to the uncinate process of the pancreas. Which part of the duodenum is most likely in direct relation to this mass?

explanation.text: The third (horizontal) part is positioned horizontally and is more likely to be in contact with structures adjacent to the pancreas. Duodenum Shortest, widest, and most fixed part of the small intestine. Extends from pylorus to duodenojejunal flexure. Shaped like a C around the head of the pancreas. Located above the level of the umbilicus, opposite the L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae. Size and Shape Length: 25 cm (10 inches). Shape: C-shaped loop.

Divided into four parts: First (superior) part: 5 cm (2 inches) Second (descending) part: 7.5 cm (3 inches) Third (horizontal) part: 10 cm (4 inches) Fourth (ascending) part: 2.5 cm (1 inch) Mostly retroperitoneal, except proximal 2.5 cm. Relations of Duodenum First Part Second Part Third Part Fourth part Anteriorly: Quadrate lobe of liver, gallbladder. Posteriorly: Portal vein, gastroduodenal artery, bile duct. Superiorly: Epiploic foramen.

Inferiorly: Head and neck of the pancreas. Anteriorly: Liver, transverse colon, small intestine. Posteriorly: Right kidney, renal vessels, IVC, psoas major. Medially: Head of the pancreas, bile duct. Laterally: Right colic flexure. Anteriorly: Superior mesenteric vessels, the root of the mesentery. Posteriorly: IVC, abdominal aorta, right ureter, gonadal vessels. Superiorly: Head of the pancreas with the uncinate process.

Inferiorly: Coils of jejunum. Anteriorly: Transverse colon, transverse mesocolon, stomach. Posteriorly: Left psoas major, left sympathetic chain, left renal artery. Superiorly: Body of pancreas. To the left: Left kidney, left ureter.
**First (superior) part (Option A):** While it is anteriorly related to the liver, it is not in direct contact with the pancreas.
**Second (descending) part (Option B):** It is adjacent to the head of the pancreas but not directly to the uncinate process.
**Fourth (ascending) part (Option D):** It is more posterior and further from the pancreas

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the ileum compared to the jejunum?

options.D: Larger and more prominent circular folds

explanation.text: The ileum has more numerous but shorter straight arteries compared to the jejunum.

Comparison of Jejunum and Ileum: Feature Jejunum Ileum Diameter Larger (4 cm external, 3 cm internal) Smaller (3 cm external, 2.5 cm internal) Wall Thickness Thicker, more vascular Thinner, less vascular (Option A) Circular Folds Deeper, more numerous Flatter, less numerous distally (Option D) Mesentery Shorter Longer Arteries Larger, with 1-3 tiers of arcades Smaller, with 2-6 tiers of arcades Straight Arteries Fewer, longer More numerous, shorter (Option C) Lymphoid Tissue Fewer Peyer's patches More Peyer’s patches, especially in terminal 25 cm (Option B) Villi Taller, more numerous Shorter, fewer towards the distal end

questions.question: A 45 y/o male patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. A CT scan reveals multiple appendices epiploicae, particularly prominent in the sigmoid colon. Which of the following statements regarding the anatomy of the large intestine is false?

options.A: The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae.
options.B: The sigmoid colon, which is S-shaped, leads directly into the rectum.
options.C: The total length of the large intestine in adults ranges from 1 to 1.5 meters.
options.D: Appendices epiploicae are more common in the distal colon.

explanation.text: The caecum is not typically 8-10 cm long, and appendices epiploicae are more prevalent in the sigmoid colon and distal colon.

Length of the Large Intestine and Its Components: Total Length of the Large intestine length in a living adult: 1 to 1.5 metres (Option C ruled out) Components of the Large Intestine: Component Description Caecum (Option A) Blind pouch at the beginning of the large intestine and is approximately 6 cm long Vermiform Appendix Narrow tube, 6-10 cm long, attached to the caecum Ascending Colon Travels upward from the caecum (20-25cm long) Right Colic Flexure Bend between ascending and transverse colon Transverse Colon Crosses the abdomen horizontally Left Colic Flexure Bend between transverse and descending colon Descending Colon Travels downward from the left colic flexure (10-15 cm long) Sigmoid Colon S-shaped segment leading to the rectum (Option B ruled out) Rectum Final straight portion, ~15 cm above the anal canal Appendices Epiploicae: Feature Details Description Small, fat-filled pouches of peritoneum on the colon's surface.
**Location Few or absent on caecum and ascending colon (Option A):** .

**More common on the distal colon (Option D ruled out):** Numerous on the sigmoid colon; can enlarge with obesity. Absent on rectum. Taeniae Coli They are are three distinct longitudinal bands of smooth muscle found in the colon. They help in peristalsis in the colon. The arrangement of Taenia coli allows for the characteristic haustra or pouches of the colon, contributing to its segmented appearance. There are 3 types: Type of Taeniae Coli Position Free Taenia Located on the antimesenteric aspect, opposite the mesentery. Omental Taenia Positioned posterolaterally. Mesocolic Taenia Positioned posteromedially, between the free taenia and the mesentery.

questions.question: What structure crosses the ureter anteriorly on both sides during its abdominal course?

explanation.text: In both males and females, the ureter is crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels during its abdominal course. These vessels are the testicular artery and vein in males and the ovarian artery and vein in females.

Relations of the abdominal part of the Ureter Anterior Relation Posterior Relation Right Ureter The second part of the Duodenum Right Colic vessels Ileocolic vessels Right testicular and ovarian vessels Root of mesentery Right Psoas Major Bifurcation of Right Common Iliac artery Left Ureter Left Colic vessels Sigmoidal vessels Left testicular and ovarian vessels Sigmoid mesocolon Left Psoas Major Bifurcation of Left Common Iliac artery Inferior mesenteric artery (Option A): The inferior mesenteric artery is a medial relation to the left ureter but does not cross it anteriorly.
**Genitofemoral nerve (Option C):** The ureter crosses anterior to the genitofemoral nerve as it travels down the abdomen, making it a posterior relation.

**Duodenum (Option D):** The descending part of the duodenum only crosses the right ureter anteriorly at its origin near the renal pelvis, but it does not cross the ureter on both sides. The left ureter is not related to the duodenum at all.

questions.question: Which vessels primarily supply the middle part of the ureter?

explanation.text: The middle part of the ureter is primarily supplied by branches from the aorta. It can also receive blood from gonadal or iliac vessels, but the aorta is the key vessel for this segment. Blood Supply of the Ureter Arteries are closely associated with the peritoneum. They form a plexus on the ureter's surface with ascending and descending branches.

The upper and middle parts receive blood from the medial side, while the pelvic part is supplied from the lateral side. Upper Part: Supplied by branches from the renal artery. (Option A ruled out) May also receive branches from gonadal or colic vessels. Middle Part: Receives branches from the aorta. Can also receive branches from gonadal or iliac vessels.
Pelvic Part: Supplied by branches from vesical, middle rectal, or uterine vessels. (Options B & C ruled out) Fig: Blood Supply of the Ureter

questions.question: A 9 y/o child presents with abdominal pain and hematuria. Imaging reveals that the left renal vein is compressed between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. What is a key anatomical feature contributing to this condition?

options.A: The left renal vein passes behind the abdominal aorta.
options.B: The pancreas lies directly posterior to the superior mesenteric artery.
options.C: The left renal vein travels behind the pancreas before crossing the aorta.
options.D: The pancreas is situated inferior to the left renal vein.

explanation.text: The left renal vein's route behind the pancreas contributes to its susceptibility to compression. Relationship of the Pancreas, Veins, and Aorta in Nutcracker Syndrome Nutcracker Syndrome: A condition caused by compression of the left renal vein leading to the left renal vein hypertension. Highlights the anatomical relationship between the pancreas, veins, and aorta.

Anatomical Features Description Left Renal Vein Originates from the hilum of the left kidney. Travels behind the pancreas and splenic vein. (Option C) (Option D ruled out) Crosses the abdominal aorta anteriorly below the superior mesenteric artery. (Option A ruled out) Nutcracker Analogy The left renal vein is compressed between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery, resembling a nutcracker. Symptoms Can lead to left renal vein hypertension.

Symptoms include hematuria and varicocele, especially in children. Pancreas' Role in Nutcracker Syndrome: Positioned directly in front of the compression site, anterior to the SMA. (Option B ruled out) Proximity to vascular structures suggests the potential to worsen the condition. The uncinate process being close to the superior mesenteric artery and vein further emphasises the pancreas's proximity to major vessels.

questions.question: Which vein receives drainage from both the left gonadal and left adrenal veins?

explanation.text: Left gonadal and left adrenal veins drain into the left renal vein, emptying into the inferior vena cava. This is a key anatomical difference from the right side, where the veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava.
**Inferior vena cava (Option A):** While the right gonadal and adrenal veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava, the left gonadal and adrenal veins drain into the left renal vein instead.

**Right renal vein (Option B):** The right renal vein handles drainage from structures on the right side of the body, such as the right kidney. It does not receive blood from the left gonadal or adrenal veins.

**Right adrenal vein (Option D):** The right adrenal vein is responsible for draining blood from the right adrenal gland into the inferior vena cava. It does not interact with the left gonadal or adrenal veins.

questions.question: Which of the following layers immediately surrounds the kidney and adheres closely to its surface?

explanation.text: The fibrous capsule, also known as the true capsule, is a thin, fibrous membrane that tightly adheres to the surface of the kidney. It is the kidney's immediate protective layer, safeguarding it from minor injuries. Internal Structure Cortex: Outer region, extends between renal pyramids as renal columns. Medulla: Contains 5-11 renal pyramids, whose apices (renal papillae) project into minor calyces.

Renal sinus: Houses renal pelvis, calyces, vessels, and fat. Calyces: Minor calyces collect urine, merging into major calyces that form the renal pelvis. Microscopic Structure Nephron: Functional unit responsible for filtering blood and producing urine, consisting of the renal corpuscle and tubule. Collecting ducts: Drain urine from nephrons into papillary ducts, which lead to the minor calyces.
**Coverings of the kidney (From inside out) Description Function Renal Capsule (Option B):** A thin, fibrous layer directly covering the kidney. Contains mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs).
**Protection, shape maintenance, stem cell niche for repair Perirenal Fat (Option D ruled out):** Adipose tissue surrounds the renal capsule (also called perinephric fat).
**Cushions and insulates the kidney Renal Fascia (Option C ruled out):** Connective tissue (Gerota's fascia) around perirenal fat, anchoring the kidney.
**Secures kidney position and separates from adjacent organs Pararenal Fat (Option A ruled out):** Outer adipose layer beyond the renal fascia. Provides additional cushioning and support

questions.question: Which structure is in direct contact with the upper pole of the right kidney?

explanation.text: The right suprarenal gland lies directly on the upper pole of the right kidney, potentially overlapping the kidney's medial border. There is no intervening peritoneum, making the gland and kidney directly connected.

Anterior Relations of Kidney Right Kidney Left Kidney The right lobe of the Liver Right suprarenal gland The second part of the duodenum Jejunum Hepatic (Right colic) flexure Left suprarenal gland Stomach Spleen Jejunum Left colic flexure Pancreas and splenic vessels The right lobe of the liver (Option A): While the right lobe of the liver covers a large portion of the anterior surface of the right kidney, they are separated by a layer of peritoneum.
**Duodenum (Option B):** The descending part of the duodenum lies against the medial side of the right kidney. However, it contacts the central portion of the kidney rather than the upper pole.
**Right colic flexure (Option D):** The right colic flexure, the junction of the ascending and transverse colon, is located inferiorly and laterally to the right kidney.

questions.question: Which rib is related to the posterior surface of the left kidney but not the right kidney?

explanation.text: The 11th rib is a posterior relation of the left kidney but not the right kidney. The right kidney is related to the 12th rib, while the left kidney is related to both the 11th and 12th ribs.

Posterior Relations of Kidney Right Kidney Left Kidney Only 12th Rib 11th Rib 12th Rib (Common to both Right and Left Kidney) Muscles: Diaphragm and in mediolateral order - Psoas Major, Quadratus Lumborum, Transversus Abdominis Ligaments: Medial and Lateral Arcuate Nerves: Subcostal, Iliohypogastric, Ilioinguinal Vessels: Subcostal 7th rib (Option A): The 7th rib is located higher in the thoracic region and does not have any direct relation to the kidneys. 8th rib (Option B): The 8th rib is positioned too high to be a posterior relation to either kidney. 12th rib (Option C): The 12th rib is related to both the right and left kidneys, not just the left kidney.
It lies posteriorly to both kidneys.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a typical site of ureteric constriction?

explanation.text: The opening of the pelvic outlet is not typically recognized as a site of ureteric constriction. Ureteric constriction occurs at the pelvic inlet (pelvic brim) where it crosses the common iliac artery. Ureteric constrictions The ureters have several points of constriction that are clinically significant, particularly for renal stone impaction. The typical sites of constriction are: 1.

Junction with the renal pelvis: This is where the ureter narrows as it transitions from the renal pelvis. (Option A ruled out) 2. At the linea terminalis: Near the medial border of the psoas major, where the ureter is kinked as it crosses the pelvic brim to enter the pelvis at the pelvic inlet. 3. Intramural segment: As the ureter pierces the bladder wall, it runs obliquely through the wall, which is the narrowest part. 4.

Crossing by ductus deferens or broad ligament: The ureter crosses underneath the ductus deferens in males and lies behind the broad ligament in females. (Option B ruled out) 5. Opening at the trigone: The ureter opens at the lateral angle of the trigone area within the urinary bladder. (Option D ruled out)

questions.question: Which part of the pancreas is covered by the peritoneum?

explanation.text: The tail of the pancreas is the only part of the pancreas that is covered by the peritoneum. It extends towards the spleen and is enclosed by the peritoneum, making it intraperitoneal. Retroperitoneal organs: Kidneys Duodenum Ascending and descending colon Rectum (lower ) Adrenal glands Ureters Head and body of Pancreas (Options A, B) Aorta and Inferior venacava

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with complaints of a progressively enlarged abdomen and discomfort on the left side. Imaging studies reveal splenomegaly. Which structure is primarily responsible for preventing the downward displacement of the spleen in this case?

explanation.text: Downward displacement of the enlarged spleen is prevented by th e phrenicolic ligament. The phrenicolic ligament connects the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. It is not attached to the spleen. However, it lies below the spleen and supports its lower pole. When the spleen gets enlarged, phrenicolic ligaments along with the splenic flexure of the colon restrict its downward displacement. Hence, it is also called Sustentaculum lienis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the autonomic innervation of the gastrointestinal tract is correct?

options.A: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the entire length of the gut.
options.B: The pelvic splanchnic nerves supply sympathetic innervation to the hindgut.
options.C: The greater splanchnic nerves provide sympathetic innervation primarily to the midgut.
options.D: The parasympathetic supply to the hindgut originates from the sacral spinal cord.

explanation.text: The parasympathetic supply to the hindgut originates from the sacral spinal cord, specifically from segments S2-S4. These fibers form the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Foregut, midgut and hindgut- Innervation Feature Foregut Midgut Hindgut Sympathetic (Preganglionic) Preganglionic fibers arise from the thoracic spinal cord (T5–T9)- and form the greater splanchnic nerves, which travel to the celiac ganglia.

Preganglionic fibers arise from the thoracic spinal cord (T10–T11) - and form the lesser splanchnic nerves, which travel to the superior mesenteric ganglion. Preganglionic fibers arise from the lumbar spinal cord (L1–L2) - and form the lumbar splanchnic nerves, which travel to the inferior mesenteric ganglion. Sympathetic (Postganglionic) Postganglionic fibers from the celiac ganglion supply the foregut organs.

These fibers follow branches of the celiac trunk to reach the target organs. Postganglionic fibers from the superior mesenteric ganglion supply the midgut organs. These fibers follow the superior mesenteric artery and its branches. Postganglionic fibers from the inferior mesenteric ganglion supply the hindgut organs. These fibers follow the inferior mesenteric artery and its branches.

Parasympathetic Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise from the vagus nerve (CN X). They pass through the celiac plexus and directly innervate the organs of the foregut. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers also arise from the vagus nerve (CN X). They pass through the superior mesenteric plexus and innervate the midgut organs. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

These fibers pass through the inferior hypogastric plexus and innervate the hindgut organs. While the vagus nerve does provide parasympathetic innervation to a large portion of the gut, it does not supply the entire length.

It innervates the foregut and midgut, extending approximately to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. (Option A) The pelvic splanchnic nerves provide parasympathetic, not sympathetic, innervation to the hindgut. (Option B) The greater splanchnic nerves primarily provide sympathetic innervation to the foregut structures, not the midgut. (Option C)

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. He reports that the pain worsens after eating and is associated with nausea. On examination, there is epigastric tenderness, but no rebound or guarding. The patient's past medical history is significant for chronic pancreatitis. You suspect autonomic involvement in his pain pattern. Which of the following nerves is most likely involved in transmitting the visceral pain signals from the pancreas?

explanation.text: Epigastric pain radiating to the back in case of chronic pancreatitis is due to autonomic innervation via the greater splanchnic nerve. Sympathetic Innervation: The nerve supply of the abdomen is primarily through the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, with the sympathetic innervation arising from the thoracic sympathetic chain.

The sympathetic fibers that supply the abdomen primarily come from the lower thoracic splanchnic nerves, which are part of the thoracic sympathetic trunk. These nerves include the greater, lesser, and least splanchnic nerves, which originate from the T5 to T12 vertebral levels. These nerves carry presynaptic sympathetic fibers that travel through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing and enter the abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves.

The greater splanchnic nerve (T5–T9) synapses in the celiac ganglion, providing sympathetic innervation to foregut derivatives, including the stomach, liver, pancreas, and parts of the small intestine.

Chronic pancreatitis can cause epigastric pain, often referred to the back due to autonomic innervation via the greater splanchnic nerve. (Option A) The lesser splanchnic nerve (T10–T11) synapses in the superior mesenteric ganglion, innervating the midgut derivatives, including the small intestine and parts of the colon. (Option B) The least splanchnic nerve (T12) innervates the kidneys via the aorticorenal ganglion.

After synapsing in the prevertebral ganglia (like the celiac, superior mesenteric, and aorticorenal ganglia), the postsynaptic fibers follow the arterial branches in peri-arterial plexuses to their target organs. Sympathetic stimulation in the abdomen primarily causes vasoconstriction and inhibits peristalsis.
This sympathetic supply is important for regulating blood flow and slowing down gastrointestinal activity, particularly during stress responses (fight or flight).
**Pelvic splanchnic nerve (Option C):** Involved in parasympathetic supply to the hindgut, not the foregut. Pain from the pancreas would not be transmitted via this nerve.
**Vagus nerve (Option D):** Primarily parasympathetic, focusing on motility
and secretions. It does not carry the sympathetic visceral pain signals from the pancreas.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with dull, poorly localized abdominal pain that began 12 hours ago. Over time, the pain becomes sharper and more localized in the right lower quadrant. The patient also reports nausea and loss of appetite. On physical examination, tenderness is noted at McBurney's point. Which of the following best explains the initial presentation of the patient's pain?

options.B: Stimulation of visceral afferent fibers accompanying sympathetic nerves
options.C: Direct irritation of somatic nerves in the abdominal wall
options.D: Referred pain via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5)

explanation.text: Referred pain occurs when visceral afferent fibers transmit pain signals to the spinal cord, which misinterprets these signals as originating from a somatic region innervated by the same spinal segment (same dermatome). Initially, the pain in appendicitis is referred to the periumbilical region due to irritation of visceral afferent fibers. These fibers travel with the sympathetic nerves (thoracolumbar flow), which innervate the small intestine.

As the inflammation progresses and the parietal peritoneum becomes involved, the pain localizes to the right lower quadrant. Unlike visceral pain, pain from structures like the parietal peritoneum is more localized and sharp. This type of pain is mediated by somatic nerves, which can pinpoint the exact area of irritation.

Referred pain and associated dermatomes: Region Dermatome Shoulder tip C4 Nipples T4 Epigastrium (Foregut pain) T7 Periumbilical (Umbilical pain) T10 Suprapubic region (Inguinal region) L1 Little toe S1 The lower limb will begin in L1 and S1 region Irritation of the peritoneum (Option A): This explains the late phase of appendicitis when the pain becomes sharp and localized due to somatic innervation of the parietal peritoneum.
However, it does not account for the initial referred pain.

**Direct irritation of somatic nerves in the abdominal wall (Option C):** Somatic nerves cause sharp, well-localized pain, as seen in later-stage appendicitis, but they do not explain the initial vague, dull pain.

**Referred pain via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) (Option D):** The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm and causes referred pain to the shoulder (e.g., from diaphragmatic irritation). It is unrelated to appendicitis or abdominal pain.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta typically bifurcate into the common iliac arteries?

explanation.text: The abdominal aorta typically bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the level of the L4 vertebra. This bifurcation point is an important anatomical landmark in the abdomen. Abdominal Aorta and Its Branches

**Vertebral Level Major Events and Branches Details T12 (Option A):** Aortic hiatus in the diaphragm Beginning of abdominal aorta Opening of the diaphragm for passage of the aorta Transition from thoracic to abdominal aorta T12-L1 Celiac artery Supplies the foregut L1 Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) Superior to the renal artery (originate at the same level) At transpyloric plane Supplies midgut L1-L2 (Option B) Renal arteries Inferior suprarenal arteries Gonadal arteries Supply kidneys Gonadal artery (Testicular or ovarian arteries) L3 Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) Supplies hindgut L4 Bifurcation Aorta divides into right and left common iliac arteries L4-L5 (Option D) Common iliac arteries Further divide into internal and external iliac arteries

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. CT angiography reveals thrombosis of a major vein draining the distal transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid colon. Which of the following veins is most likely to be affected in this patient's condition?

explanation.text: The patient's symptoms and the affected area (distal transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid colon) indicate an issue with the hindgut and its blood supply. Hindgut is drained by inferior mesenteric vein.

Feature Foregut Midgut Hindgut Embryological Origin Derived from the cranial part of the primitive gut tube Derived from the middle part of the primitive gut tube Derived from the caudal part of the primitive gut tube Main Organs/Structures Esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and first and second parts of the duodenum Second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colon Distal 1/3 of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, upper part of the anal canal Arterial Supply Celiac trunk (Celiac artery) Superior mesenteric artery Inferior mesenteric artery Venous Drainage Drains into the portal vein via the splenic vein and its tributaries Drains into the portal vein via the superior mesenteric vein Drains into the portal vein via the inferior mesenteric vein Lymphatic Drainage Celiac lymph nodes Superior mesenteric lymph nodes Inferior mesenteric lymph nodes Nerve Supply Sympathetic: Greater splanchnic nerves (T5–T9); Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve Sympathetic: Lesser splanchnic nerves (T10–T11); Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve Sympathetic: Lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1–L2); Parasympathetic: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the innervation and vascular supply of the uterus and vagina is correct?

options.A: The parasympathetic supply to the entire uterus and vagina comes from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4)
options.B: The uterine artery is a branch of the external iliac artery
options.C: The vaginal venous plexus drains primarily into the internal pudendal vein
options.D: The superior part of the vagina receives its arterial supply from the vaginal artery, while the inferior part is supplied by branches of the internal pudendal artery

explanation.text: The superior part of the vagina receives its arterial supply from the vaginal artery, while branches of the internal pudendal artery supply the inferior part.

The neurovascular supply of the female reproductive system is given in the table below: Neurovascular supply of the female reproductive system Structure Arterial Supply Venous Drainage Sympathetic Innervation Parasympathetic Innervation Uterus Uterine artery (branch of internal iliac artery) Uterine venous plexus to internal iliac veins T12-L2 via superior hypogastric plexus Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) Upper 2/3 of Vagina Vaginal artery (branch of internal iliac artery) Vaginal venous plexus to internal iliac veins T12-L2 via inferior hypogastric plexus Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) Lower 1/3 of Vagina Branches of internal pudendal artery Vaginal venous plexus to internal iliac veins Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) While the parasympathetic supply to the uterus and upper 2/3 of the vagina comes from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4), the lower 1/3 of the vagina receives parasympathetic innervation via the pudendal nerve. (Option A) The uterine artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery, not the external iliac artery. (Option B) The vaginal venous plexus drains primarily into the internal iliac veins, not the internal pudendal vein. (Option C)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about pre-aortic and para-aortic lymph nodes is correct?

options.A: Pre-aortic nodes primarily drain lymph from the lower limbs
options.B: Para-aortic nodes are located posterior to the abdominal aorta
options.C: Coeliac nodes are a subset of pre-aortic nodes
options.D: Lateral aortic nodes drain lymph from the stomach and pancreas

explanation.text: Coeliac nodes are a constituent of the pre-aortic group of lymph nodes. Pre-aortic nodes can be subdivided into coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric nodes. Pre-aortic and para-aortic lymph nodes

Lymph Node Group Location Primary Drainage Subgroups Pre-aortic nodes Anterior to the abdominal aorta Gastrointestinal viscera including pancreas, liver, spleen Coeliac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric nodes Para-aortic nodes (Lateral aortic) On either side of the abdominal aorta Deep layers of body wall, retroperitoneal pelvic viscera, gonads (testes and ovaries) Left and right lumbar (of the kidney), aortocaval, retrocaval, precaval groups Pre-aortic nodes primarily drain lymph from gastrointestinal viscera, not the lower limbs. (Option A) Para-aortic nodes (also called lateral aortic nodes) are located on either side of the abdominal aorta, not posterior to it. (Option B) Lateral aortic nodes (para-aortic) primarily drain lymph from the deep layers of the body wall, retroperitoneal pelvic viscera, and gonads. (Option D).
The stomach and pancreas are primarily drained by pre-aortic nodes (specifically coeliac and superior mesenteric nodes).
